## Recommendation

On paper, the best option is to clean the hulls, recover kernels, and sell the cleaned hulls to the local dairy. It nets about $98,000 for the lot ($98 per ton), against $85,000 ($85 per ton) for selling straight to the local dairy. That is $13,000 more ($13 per ton).

Treat this as a lean, not a decision. The gain depends on placeholder numbers for cleaning cost, kernel value, and distance. Selling to the local dairy is the safe fallback, since it is an established market and uses sourced prices.

## How the options compare

Net is per ton after hauling and processing, with kernel value included where it applies. The range runs low to high.

| Option | Net per ton (low–high) | Expected net, 1,000 tons |
|---|---|---|
| Clean, recover kernels, sell to local dairy | $80–$116 | $98,000 |
| Sell to local dairy (baseline) | $70–$100 | $85,000 |
| Distant dairy market | $41–$71 | $56,000 |
| Bioenergy feedstock | $7–$27 | $17,000 |
| Compost or soil amendment | $6–$26 | $16,000 |
| Hull powder food ingredient | No price | Not ranked |

The dairy feed price of $76–$106 per ton is sourced [giannini2026], and so is the hauling rate of $0.30 per ton-mile. Distances, cleaning cost, and kernel value are placeholders. The distant dairy price, bioenergy, and compost values are placeholders too.

The food ingredient option has no price, so I have not ranked it. A buyer quote would need to beat $175 per ton to cover its processing and hauling costs. That is a placeholder-based figure. [gras2026] says hull powder is judged safe for human food but has no public price.

## What could change the answer

- **Cleaning cost.** The cleaning option beats the baseline only if its cost and kernel value hold up. It would still be worthwhile if the local dairy price were below $78 per ton, its break-even. Get an equipment or toll-cleaning quote.
- **Dairy price swings.** Hull prices have ranged from about $60 per ton in a slump to $130 per ton [farmprogress_low, wcngg2022]. About 97% of hulls go to dairy rations, so buyers have leverage [farmprogress_low].
- **Distant dairy.** It would need about $160 per ton to match the local dairy, well above its placeholder range. Freight can erase the premium.
- **Bioenergy and compost.** Their placeholder prices are far below what they would need to compete, so they only make sense if a real quote is much higher.

## Quality and risk checks

- **Aflatoxin is untested.** Test before selling for feed or food. This applies to every option that goes to feed or food.
- **Moisture and crude fiber are not entered.** Dairy buyers follow the CDFA standard of crude fiber below 15% [wcngg2022]. Test both before committing. Cleaned hulls must also still meet that standard.
- **Kernel recovery.** Recovered kernels may grade lower than standard kernels. About 1–1.3% of hull-pile weight is recoverable kernel [abc_food2025].
- **Equipment.** The cleaning option needs access to cleaning and kernel-recovery equipment.

## Assumptions and sources

Sourced: the dairy feed price range, the hauling rate, the fiber standard, and the price history. Placeholder: all distances, cleaning and processing costs, kernel value, and the prices for distant dairy, bioenergy, compost, and food. Because of this, the ranking depends on placeholder values.

- [abc_food2025] Almond Board of California, "Unlocking New Value: Commercializing Almond Hulls as Food Ingredients": https://www.almonds.org/almond-industry/industry-news/unlocking-new-value-commercializing-almond-hulls-food-ingredients
- [farmprogress_low] Farm Progress, "Almond hulls – Low prices call for expanded markets": https://www.farmprogress.com/tree-nuts/almond-hulls-low-prices-call-for-expanded-markets
- [giannini2026] UC Giannini Foundation, "Almond Shell Circularity in California's Bioeconomy" (2026): https://s.giannini.ucop.edu/uploads/pub/2026/06/26/v29n5_3_mg7Nqvg.pdf
- [gras2026] AgInfo, "Unlocking New Uses for Almond Hulls": https://www.aginfo.net/report/65481/32/Unlocking-New-Uses-for-Almond-Hulls
- [wcngg2022] WCNGG, "Almond Hull Prices are a Bright Spot" (2022): https://wcngg.com/2022/04/18/almond-hull-prices-are-a-bright-spot-for-the-almond-industry/

These are estimates. Confirm prices with buyer quotes and test hull quality before deciding.

## Recommendation

Don't commit this lot to a feed buyer yet. At 16% crude fiber, the hulls fail the 15% feed standard [wcngg2022]. That rules out local dairy, distant dairy, and clean-and-recover as the lot stands. Aflatoxin has not been tested, and moisture is not entered.

Of the options that pass the quality check, bioenergy ranks first at about $17 per ton expected, or $17,000 for the lot. Compost or soil amendment is close behind at $16 per ton, or $16,000. Both rest entirely on placeholder prices, so treat this as a fallback, not a plan. Hull powder for food is eligible but has no price, so it is not ranked.

The practical next step is to test the fiber, aflatoxin, and moisture. Then get quotes. If a re-test or cleaning brings fiber under 15%, local dairy becomes the benchmark again.

## How the options compare

Net is per short ton, after hauling and processing. Local dairy is the baseline.

| Option | Eligible | Expected net/ton | Expected total | Price basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bioenergy | Yes | $17 | $17,000 | Placeholder |
| Compost/soil | Yes | $16 | $16,000 | Placeholder |
| Clean and recover | No (fiber) | $98 | $98,000 | Price sourced, cleaning and kernel value placeholder |
| Local dairy | No (fiber) | $85 | $85,000 | Price sourced, miles placeholder |
| Distant dairy | No (fiber) | $56 | $56,000 | Price placeholder |
| Food ingredient | Yes | Needs quote | None | No price |

The feed options look better on paper, but they are not open to this lot at 16% fiber. The local dairy price range of $76–106 per ton is sourced [giannini2026]. The hauling rate of $0.30 per ton-mile is also sourced. Distances are placeholders.

For food ingredient, a buyer would need to pay at least $175 per ton to break even. That is after $60 per ton processing and $30 per ton hauling, both placeholders. Hull powder is judged safe for human food, but there is no public price [gras2026].

## What could change the answer

- **Fiber result:** If a re-test or cleaning gets fiber below 15%, local dairy ($85 per ton expected) beats both eligible options by a wide margin. Clean-and-recover would show $98 per ton, but only if cleaned hulls pass and the kernel value holds up. That value is a placeholder.
- **Buyer quotes:** Bioenergy would need to pay well above its $25–45 per ton placeholder range to compete with dairy. Its break-even against local dairy is $103 per ton. Compost is $99 per ton.
- **Food quote:** Only a quote of $175 per ton or more would make food worth pursuing.
- **Dairy price swings:** Prices have ranged from about $60 per ton to $130 per ton [farmprogress_low, wcngg2022]. About 97% of hulls go to dairy rations, so buyers have leverage [farmprogress_low].

## Quality and risk checks

- **Crude fiber:** 16% is at or above the 15% CDFA feed standard [wcngg2022]. All three feed options are flagged ineligible.
- **Aflatoxin:** Untested. Test before selling for feed or food.
- **Moisture:** Not entered. Hulls are typically delivered at 88–91% dry matter [wcngg2022].
- **Placeholders:** Bioenergy and compost carry the warning that all values are demo placeholders. Both also need a willing local taker.
- **Distant dairy:** Rail to Texas has precedent, but the premium is not guaranteed [farmprogress_low]. Freight can erase it.

## Assumptions and sources

Sourced: the hauling rate, the local dairy price range, the feed fiber standard, and the price history. Placeholder: most miles, processing costs, kernel recovery value, and the bioenergy, compost, distant dairy, and food prices. Because of this, every ranked result depends on placeholder values.

- [farmprogress_low] Farm Progress, "Almond hulls – Low prices call for expanded markets": https://www.farmprogress.com/tree-nuts/almond-hulls-low-prices-call-for-expanded-markets

- [wcngg2022] WCNGG, "Almond Hull Prices are a Bright Spot" (2022): https://wcngg.com/2022/04/18/almond-hull-prices-are-a-bright-spot-for-the-almond-industry/

Sell the 1,000 tons to the local dairy. It has the best expected result: about $85 per ton, or $85,000 in total, after hauling. The range is $70,000 to $100,000. The local dairy is an established outlet and the other options don't beat it on the numbers we have.

## How the options compare

Net figures are per ton after hauling and processing.

| Option | Expected net/ton | Expected total | vs. local dairy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Local dairy | $85 | $85,000 | baseline |
| Clean, recover kernels, sell to dairy | $75 | $75,000 | -$10,000 |
| Distant dairy | $56 | $56,000 | -$29,000 |
| Bioenergy | $17 | $17,000 | -$68,000 |
| Compost/soil | $16 | $16,000 | -$69,000 |
| Food ingredient | no price | no price | not ranked |

- **Distant dairy:** the $116–$146 price is a placeholder. Freight of $75 per ton eats the premium. It would need $160 per ton to break even.
- **Bioenergy and compost:** all values are placeholders, and both come in far behind.
- **Food ingredient:** no public price exists [gras2026], so it is not ranked or recommended. A buyer quote would need to beat $175 per ton to break even. That figure includes a placeholder processing cost of $60 per ton.

judge_issues: "A buyer would need to offer more than $199 per ton to break even": this misstates the figure. In the payload, break_even_price_per_ton is the price needed to match the local dairy's $79/ton net, not to reach zero net. "so it is not ranked or recommended": the payload does rank the food ingredient (rank 6). It is flagged needs_quote, with no net values. Say it is ranked last because it has no price, not that it is unranked.

The break-even framing is inconsistent across the report. Compost and bioenergy are correctly described as needing $102/$115 "to match the dairy". Food ingredient and distant dairy use the same kind of figure but call it "break even". ## Recommendation

Clean the hulls, recover the leftover kernels, then sell to the local dairy. This ranks first at about $94 per ton expected, or about $112,980 for the 1,200 tons. That is $8 per ton (about $9,060) more than selling straight to the local dairy at $87 per ton net ($103,920). judge_issues: "Its break-even price is $84 per ton, so it beats selling straight to the dairy at that price." This misreads the payload. A break-even price of $84.45 is the dairy price at which the cleaning option only matches the baseline's current $86.60 net. It ties at that price; it does not beat it.

The bullet headed "Cleaning cost" never discusses cleaning cost. It says "The option stays ahead as long as the dairy price holds," but a dairy price drop lowers both feed options equally, so the $7.55/ton edge stays. The real risk is the cleaning cost, which the payload calls a demo placeholder. The report should say the option stays ahead only while cleaning plus lost margin stays under roughly $7.55/ton more than assumed.

"The data note says placeholder values do not affect the ranking" is followed directly by "The cleaning cost is described as a demo placeholder." The report does not reconcile these two statements, which may confuse the reader about how solid the first-place result is.
Recommendation: "That is $8 per ton" is rounded from $7.55. It is acceptable, but the narrow margin should be stated precisely, since a small cost change could flip the result.
The Recommendation names the weakest inputs but does not give the next concrete step, such as getting a cleaning quote before committing. That step appears only later in the report.
